title: Poison Control Centers: A Good Thing
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and function of poison control centers, from the pre-industrial era through the Industrial Revolution's household chemicals, early food and drug regulation (Harvey Wiley's Poison Squad, the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act, the 1938 sulfanilamide elixir disaster), the Federal Caustic Poison Act, and Chevalier Jackson's campaign against lye ingestion. They cover Louis Dolman's Chicago index-card hotline and the early consolidated centers, the shift to direct public calls in 1961, Surgeon General Leroy Burney's National Clearinghouse, Poisindex, the National Poison Data System, the Mr. Yuck campaign, consolidation to 55 centers, the 2001 toll-free number 1-800-222-1222, how calls are handled and followed up, CDC toxicosurveillance and sentinel events, the 2016-era Tide Pod gap, and current statistics on who gets poisoned and by what. The episode also includes banter, a listener mail corrections segment, and a plug for a six ft Under anniversary episode.
topics: National Clearinghouse for Poison Control Centers

entities.name: National Clearinghouse for Poison Control Centers
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

segments.title: Opening banter and poisoning jokes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about jokes, movies, and Pumping Iron, then Josh introduces the topic of poison control centers and how they work.

segments.title: Pre-industrial poisons and the rise of household chemicals
segments.summary: The hosts argue that poison control is a recent invention because household chemicals and mass-market poisons appeared with the Industrial Revolution, and they discuss look-alike products that cause accidental poisoning.

segments.title: Early food and drug regulation
segments.summary: The hosts cover late nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century regulation, including Harvey Wiley and the Poison Squad, muckraking journalists, the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, and the 1930s sulfanilamide elixir disaster that led to pre-market testing requirements.

segments.title: Break and promotion
segments.summary: A short break, followed by a host plug for an Alan Ball six ft Under anniversary episode.

segments.title: Lye ingestion and the Federal Caustic Poison Act
segments.summary: Chevalier Jackson, a laryngologist, campaigned against children swallowing lye. The Federal Caustic Poison Act of 1927 required warning labels on caustic poisons. A Duke pediatrician then began cataloging poisons more broadly in the 1930s.

segments.title: Louis Dolman and the first poison hotline
segments.summary: Louis Dolman, a Chicago pharmacist, collected poison data on index cards and ran a day-and-night phone hotline in the 1940s. He and a partner founded early poison centers, which were later consolidated, and the field became data-driven.

segments.title: Direct public calls, National Clearinghouse, and national databases
segments.summary: Direct public calls to poison centers began in 1961. Surgeon General Leroy Burney founded the National Clearinghouse for Poison Control Centers. Poisindex appeared in 1974, and the National Poison Data System was built over time.

segments.title: Seventies and eighties: child-resistant packaging and the Mr. Yuck campaign
segments.summary: Child-resistant prescription pill packaging in 1974 reduced child pill poisonings, shifting focus toward adult poisoning. The Mr. Yuck campaign in Pittsburgh replaced the skull and crossbones with a sickly green face.

segments.title: Consolidation, toll-free number, and how calls are handled
segments.summary: Poison centers consolidated from about 650 to 55 centers, and a single national toll-free number, 1-800-222-1222, was introduced around 2001. Specialists handle calls, may reroute callers, coordinate hospital care, and follow up. Calls are logged in the National Poison Data System, which the CDC uses for toxicosurveillance and sentinel events such as the 1996 heroin case.

segments.title: Statistics, Tide Pod gap, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Tide Pod poisoning data gaps, current poisoning statistics by age and intent, and close with listener mail corrections and the sign-off.
